A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Steerable Transformers research by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison despite the revised title and organization.

before.justification: v1 reports original Rotated MNIST and ModelNet10 classification experiments, including repeated-run results, architecture comparisons, and attention visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains original classification results and adds original PH2 skin-lesion and BraTS brain-tumor segmentation results and prediction examples.

M1.justification: The stated method replaces exponential radial positional weighting with inverse-square weighting, adds positional encoding to value vectors, and replaces general scalar mixing of frequency-wise attention with one shared frequency-summed attention distribution. The normalization denominator also gains a square root. v2 additionally introduces a steerable U-net segmentation architecture with skip connections and interpolation.

E1.justification: v2 adds PH2 dermoscopic skin-lesion segmentation and BraTS multimodal MRI tumor segmentation, substantially extending both task and medical-domain coverage. Rotated MNIST classification and ModelNet10 classification under z-axis and SO(3) rotations are retained.

E2.justification: The MNIST comparison expands from three attention comparators to include SVM, TIRBM, TI-Pooling, P4CNN, Harmonic Net, RotEqNet, Weiler et al. (2018b), and E2CNN. Conversely, the same-backbone 'Without Transformer' comparator disappears from both classification datasets. The external ModelNet10 comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The new segmentation evaluations introduce Dice scoring excluding background, PH2 splits of 100/50/50 and BraTS splits of 243/96/145 for training/validation/testing, and 100-epoch training with batch size 1. For retained MNIST experiments, the reported batch size changes from 100 to 25. Classification splits and ModelNet10's 12-view test-time augmentation are retained.

E4.justification: The radial-resolution/Fourier-cutoff sensitivity comparisons and attention-equivariance visualization remain. v2 removes the direct transformer-removal ablation using an otherwise identical backbone, but adds qualitative segmentation examples comparing ground truth, predictions, and probability maps in Figures 3 and 5.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over five runs for their principal architecture comparisons. v2 extends this practice to segmentation without introducing a different uncertainty procedure, seed-reporting practice, confidence interval, or significance test.

E6.justification: v2 adds segmentation results: PH2 Dice at k=8 is 90.72 for the transformer versus 89.63 for convolution; BraTS scores are 75.01/54.89/76.37 versus 73.29/51.07/74.43. Retained classification accuracies are numerically unchanged, while some parameter counts change, including MNIST convolution at k=4, r=4 from 1.98M to 1.18M. Transformer-removal results disappear and additional MNIST baseline results appear.

T1.justification: The equivariance proposition is retained, but Appendix B revises its derivation for shared attention and position-dependent values. New Section 3.5 derives an asymptotic comparison with convolutions under N much smaller than C and fixed kernels. The printed softmax and normalization definitions are also revised; Appendix A's mathematical background is substantially unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of SE(d)-equivariant Fourier-space attention, integration with steerable convolutions, and improved performance in two and three dimensions. Volumetric grids receive stronger emphasis, but were already the input setting in v1. The medical-imaging potential claim is retained with additional supporting experiments.

C2.justification: v2 adds arguments that treating dense volumes as point clouds can discard useful grid structure and introduce unsuitable biases and memory costs. Appendix C.1 attributes stronger Weiler/E2CNN results to higher Fourier cutoffs and resource constraints. v1's suggestion that enlarging convolutional networks causes overfitting is removed; the general attention-memory limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendices C.3–C.4 add segmentation data links, interpolation and output details, feature ratios, hyperparameters, hardware, and training times. Conversely, v1's layer-by-layer classification architectures in Figures 4–5 and angular-resolution setting of 40 are removed. MNIST training resources are revised from four 16GB GPUs for 2.5 hours to one 16GB GPU for four hours.

R1.justification: Related work expands to Equiformer, Equiformerv2, efficient SO(3)-to-SO(2) convolutions, graph attention, and early convolutional encoders, alongside additional benchmark and segmentation references. The contribution discussion develops a substantial distinction between dense volumetric grids and sparse point clouds and between hybrid and standalone attention architectures. Publication updates to existing citations are not new works.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental narrative are substantially reorganized and rewritten. Related Work becomes an introduction subsection, a dedicated Our Contribution subsection appears, external classification comparisons move into Appendix C, and detailed architecture listings are replaced by prose. The title becomes 'Steerable Transformers for Volumetric Data.'

P2.justification: The main text changes from one column to two columns. Tables are restructured for segmentation metrics and broader MNIST comparisons. New segmentation Figures 3 and 5 replace the former architecture listings as substantial visual content. The ModelNet10 example figure and external comparison table move to the appendix, while the attention schematic and equivariance visualization are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies direct medical-segmentation evidence for an application only suggested in v1 and places MNIST results alongside stronger convolutional baselines, improving empirical support and comparative balance. These gains are tempered by removing the matched-backbone transformer-removal control and detailed classification architectures. Ambiguous depth descriptions—two transformer blocks in Section 4 versus a single layer in Appendix C—also limit reproducibility, preventing a larger overall improvement.
